title: What is the Repository pattern (and how does it relate to DAO) — abstracting data access behind an interface so business logic does not depend on the persistence technology, enabling a swappable store and easy mocking in tests — and why keep queries out of controllers/services?

s1_definition.profdef: The Repository pattern abstracts data access behind a clean interface — the service layer calls `tradeRepo.findSettledByAccountId(accountId)` without knowing whether the data comes from PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, or an in-memory map. The interface defines WHAT data is needed; the implementation decides HOW to get it. DAO (Data Access Object) is the older pattern with the same goal but typically exposes lower-level methods (SQL, JDBC). Spring Data's Repository takes it further: you define an interface, Spring auto-generates the implementation. Benefits: (1) SWAPPABLE STORE — switch from JPA to MongoDB by changing the implementation, not the service. (2) TESTABILITY — mock the repository interface in unit tests without a database. (3) SEPARATION — queries live in the repository, not scattered in controllers/services. (4) SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY — service handles business logic, repository handles data access.
s1_definition.analogy: The service says "give me all settled trades for Rajesh" — it doesn't care if the clerk looks in a filing cabinet (PostgreSQL), a digital ledger (MongoDB), or a memory cache (Redis). The Repository is the COUNTER WINDOW: the service walks up and asks for data. Behind the counter, the implementation handles the details. DAO is like an older counter that still works but shows more plumbing (raw SQL visible). Keeping queries out of controllers is like keeping kitchen work out of the dining room — clean separation.
s1_definition.oneliner: Repository = interface abstraction over persistence. Service depends on interface, not implementation. Swappable DB, mockable tests, clean separation. DAO = older equivalent. Queries stay in repository, not controller/service.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Repository pattern abstracts data access behind a clean interface — the service layer calls `tradeRepo.findSettledByAccountId(accountId)` without knowing whether the data comes from PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, or an in-memory map. The interface defines WHAT data is needed; the implementation decides HOW to get it. DAO (Data Access Object) is the older pattern with the same goal but typically exposes lower-level methods (SQL, JDBC). Spring Data's Repository takes it further: you define an interface, Spring auto-generates the implementation. Benefits: (1) SWAPPABLE STORE — switch from JPA to MongoDB by changing the implementation, not the service. (2) TESTABILITY — mock the repository interface in unit tests without a database. (3) SEPARATION — queries live in the repository, not scattered in controllers/services. (4) SINGLE RESPONSIBILITY — service handles business logic, repository handles data access.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The service says "give me all settled trades for Rajesh" — it doesn't care if the clerk looks in a filing cabinet (PostgreSQL), a digital ledger (MongoDB), or a memory cache (Redis). The Repository is the COUNTER WINDOW: the service walks up and asks for data. Behind the counter, the implementation handles the details. DAO is like an older counter that still works but shows more plumbing (raw SQL visible). Keeping queries out of controllers is like keeping kitchen work out of the dining room — clean separation.

**One line to remember:** Repository = interface abstraction over persistence. Service depends on interface, not implementation. Swappable DB, mockable tests, clean separation. DAO = older equivalent. Queries stay in repository, not controller/service.

sections.s3_banking:
**Problem — The bank's settlement service has EntityManager queries scattered across controllers, services, and utility classes.** 47 JPQL queries in 12 files. When the team needed to add a Redis cache layer, they had to modify ALL 12 files. When writing unit tests, every test required a real database (Testcontainers — slow). The team refactors: ALL queries move into TradeRepository interface. Service depends on the interface. Controllers call services. Unit tests mock the repository. Adding Redis caching now requires only a new implementation of the same interface — zero service changes.

**What the project will show:** Repository interface with Spring Data auto-implementation, service depending on interface (not JPA), controller calling service (no query logic), unit test with mocked repository (no DB), and the layered architecture: Controller → Service → Repository → Database.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** GET /settlement/summary/SAV2001. Controller calls `service.getSettlementSummary("SAV2001")`. Controller knows NOTHING about persistence.

**Step 2.** Service calls `tradeRepo.findByAccountIdAndStatus("SAV2001", "SETTLED")`. Service depends on TradeRepository INTERFACE — not JPA, not EntityManager, not SQL.

**Step 3.** Spring Data's auto-generated implementation translates method name to JPQL: `SELECT t FROM Trade t WHERE t.accountId = ?1 AND t.status = ?2`. Hibernate generates SQL for PostgreSQL dialect.

**Step 4.** Two settled trades returned. Service calculates total: 245050 + 176000 = 421050. Business logic stays in service. Query logic stays in repository.

**Step 5.** In unit test: `when(tradeRepo.findByAccountIdAndStatus(...)).thenReturn(List.of(trade1, trade2))` — repository is MOCKED. No database. Test runs in 10ms. The service is tested in isolation — only its business logic (summation) is verified.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ LAYERED ARCHITECTURE ═══

  Controller ──→ Service ──→ Repository ──→ Database
  (HTTP)         (Business)   (Data Access)   (PostgreSQL)

  Controller: parses request, calls service, formats response
  Service: business logic (calculate total, apply rules)
  Repository: data access (queries, persistence)
  Database: stores data

  Each layer depends ONLY on the layer below it.
  Each layer is independently testable:
    Controller: @WebMvcTest (mock service)
    Service: @MockBean or Mockito (mock repository)
    Repository: @DataJpaTest (real JPA, in-memory DB)

  ═══ REPOSITORY vs DAO ═══

  REPOSITORY (Spring Data):           DAO (traditional):
  ├─ Interface — Spring generates impl ├─ Class with SQL/JDBC code
  ├─ Method name → query               ├─ Explicit SQL strings
  ├─ Technology-agnostic interface      ├─ JDBC/JPA-specific implementation
  ├─ DDD-oriented (collection of objects)├─ Data access-oriented (CRUD)
  └─ Highly mockable (interface)        └─ Mockable but heavier

  ═══ WHY QUERIES STAY IN REPOSITORY ═══

  (Avoid) Query in controller: controller changes when DB changes
  (Avoid) Query in service: service mixes business logic + data access
  (Recommended) Query in repository: ONLY repository changes when DB changes
     Service: business logic only. Controller: HTTP only.
```

```
                              ┌────────────┐      ┌────────────┐
                              │ PostgreSQL │      │ MongoDB /  │  ← Data Layer
                              │ (primary)  │      │ in-memory  │  (swap behind iface)
                              └────────────┘      └────────────┘

  Repository = collection-like, domain-centric abstraction over persistence.
  DAO = lower-level CRUD-per-table; Repository hides the store from the domain.
  Observability: repository call metrics decoupled from concrete JDBC/Mongo.
  Security: single boundary to enforce tenant/row filters before data access.
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Repository pattern abstracts data access behind an interface so the service layer depends on the abstraction, not the implementation. The service calls `tradeRepo.findSettledByAccountId(accountId)` without knowing if the data comes from PostgreSQL, MongoDB, or Redis. This enables three things: swappable persistence technology (change the implementation, not the service), easy mocking in unit tests (mock the interface, no database needed), and clean separation of concerns (queries in repository, business logic in service, HTTP in controller).

In my settlement service, the SettlementService depends on TradeRepository interface — it has zero imports of JPA, EntityManager, or SQL. The unit test mocks the repository with Mockito and tests business logic (total calculation) in 10ms without any database. The integration test uses @DataJpaTest to verify the actual JPA queries against H2. If the team later adds Redis caching, they create a new implementation of the same interface — the service doesn't change.

DAO and Repository serve the same purpose — abstracting data access. DAO is the older, more generic term. Repository is DDD-oriented, acting as a collection of domain objects. With Spring Data, the distinction is mostly theoretical: `JpaRepository` extends `CrudRepository` and provides both DAO-level CRUD and Repository-level domain abstraction. The key principle: keep queries in the repository layer, business logic in the service layer, and HTTP concerns in the controller layer. Each layer is independently testable.
